en energikilde.explanation: "En energikilde" means "an energy source". It is built from "energi" (energy) and "kilde" (source). To talk about water coming out of the ground, "kilde" also means a spring: "en kilde i skoven" (a spring in the forest).

en eng.explanation: "En eng" means "a meadow". To talk about a meadow with wild flowers, say: "Der er blomster på engen" (There are flowers in the meadow). To talk about a field where a farmer grows crops, use "en mark" (a field): "Bonden pløjer marken" (The farmer ploughs the field).

en engel.explanation: "En engel" means "an angel". To say someone is very kind, call them an angel, as in English: "Du er en engel!" (You are an angel!).

en englænder.explanation: "En englænder" means "an Englishman". It comes from the country name "England". To say what language he speaks, use "engelsk" (English): "Han taler engelsk" (He speaks English).

en enhed.explanation: "En enhed" means "a device". To talk about a unit of measurement, "enhed" also means "a unit": "En meter er en enhed for længde" (A meter is a unit of length).

en enke.explanation: "En enke" means "a widow". To say a woman's husband died and she is now a widow, use "blive enke" (become a widow): "Hun blev enke sidste år" (She became a widow last year).

en enkeltbillet.explanation: "En enkeltbillet" means "a one-way ticket". It is built from "enkelt" (single) and "billet" (ticket). To ask for a ticket for the trip there and back, say "en returbillet" (a round-trip ticket): "Jeg vil gerne have en returbillet" (I would like a round-trip ticket).

en enlig forsørger.explanation: "En enlig forsørger" means "a single parent". It is built from "enlig" (single, alone) and "en forsørger" (a provider). To say someone pays for a family, use "forsørger": "Han er forsørger for tre børn" (He is the provider for three children).

en entré.explanation: "En entré" means "a hallway". Write it with the accent on the last letter, "entré", not "entre". To say it costs nothing to get in, use "entré" for the admission fee: "Der er gratis entré" (Admission is free).

en epidemi.explanation: "En epidemi" means "an epidemic". To talk about an outbreak that spreads across the whole world, use "en pandemi" (a pandemic): "Pandemien ramte hele verden" (The pandemic hit the whole world).

en episode.explanation: "En episode" means "an episode". To say you watch an episode, use "at se" (to watch): "Vi ser en episode i aften" (We are watching an episode tonight).

en erfaring.explanation: "En erfaring" means "experience", as in skill you gain from doing a job. To talk about one event you lived through, use "en oplevelse" (an experience): "Turen var en stor oplevelse" (The trip was a great experience).

en ergoterapeut.explanation: "En ergoterapeut" means "an occupational therapist". To say who helps you cook and dress after an injury, say: "Ergoterapeuten hjælper mig med at lave mad" (The occupational therapist helps me cook). To talk about the therapist who trains your muscles, use "en fysioterapeut" (a physical therapist): "Fysioterapeuten træner min skulder" (The physical therapist trains my shoulder).

en erhvervsuddannelse.explanation: "En erhvervsuddannelse" means "a vocational education". It is built from "erhverv" (trade) and "uddannelse" (education). To say you study for a trade, use "at tage" (to take): "Han tager en erhvervsuddannelse som tømrer" (He is taking a vocational education as a carpenter).

en erindring.explanation: "En erindring" means "a memory". To talk about a book a person writes about their own life, use the plural "erindringer" (memoirs): "Han har skrevet sine erindringer" (He has written his memoirs).

en erkendelse.explanation: "En erkendelse" means "a realization". It comes from the verb "at erkende" (to acknowledge). To talk about admitting you did wrong, use "erkendelse af skyld" (admission of guilt).

en erklæring.explanation: "En erklæring" means "a declaration / statement". It comes from the verb "at erklære" (to declare). To say what a declaration is about, add "om" (about): "en erklæring om samtykke" (a declaration of consent).

en erstatning.explanation: "En erstatning" means "compensation / a replacement". To talk about money you get for damage, use it for "compensation": "Jeg fik erstatning for skaden" (I received compensation for the damage). To talk about someone or something that takes another's place, use it for "a replacement": "Vi leder efter en erstatning for ham" (We are looking for a replacement for him).

en etage.explanation: "En etage" means "a floor (story)", as in a level of a building. To talk about the surface you walk on, use "et gulv" (a floor): "Gulvet er koldt" (The floor is cold).

en etagebolig.explanation: "En etagebolig" means "an apartment in a multi-story building". It is built from "etage" (floor) and "bolig" (home). To talk about any place where you live, use "en bolig" (a home): "Vi søger en ny bolig" (We are looking for a new home).

en euro.explanation: "En euro" means "a euro". After a number, "euro" does not change: "Det koster fem euro" (It costs five euros). Denmark does not use the euro. Danish money is "en krone" (a krone): "Det koster tyve kroner" (It costs twenty kroner).

en europæer.explanation: "En europæer" means "a European". It comes from the continent's name "Europa" (Europe). To describe things from Europe, use "europæisk" (European): "europæisk historie" (European history).

en evakuering.explanation: "En evakuering" means "an evacuation". It comes from the verb "at evakuere" (to evacuate). To say people must leave a place, say: "Vi skal evakuere bygningen" (We must evacuate the building).

en evighed.explanation: "En evighed" means "an eternity". To say something took a very long time, use it as in English: "Det varede en evighed" (It took forever).

en evne.explanation: "En evne" means "an ability". To talk about a skill you learn by practising, use "en færdighed" (a skill): "Hun har lært en ny færdighed" (She has learned a new skill).

end.explanation: "End" means "than". To compare two things, put it after a word like "større" (bigger): "Hun er højere end mig" (She is taller than me). To say two things are equal, use "som" (as) instead: "Han er lige så høj som mig" (He is as tall as me).

endda.explanation: "Endda" means "even". To add a stronger word to what you just said, say "ja endda" (indeed even): "Maden er god, ja endda fremragende" (The food is good, indeed even excellent).

endelig.explanation: "Endelig" means "finally". When something you have waited for happens, say: "Endelig!" (At last!). Do not mix it up with "endeligt" (for good), which has a t: "Datoen er endeligt fastsat" (The date is set for good).

endeligt.explanation: "Endeligt" means "for good". Do not mix it up with "endelig" (finally), which has no t: "Endelig kom toget" (The train finally came).

endnu.explanation: "Endnu" means "yet / still". To answer that you have not done something yet, say: "Har du spist?" "Nej, ikke endnu" (Have you eaten? No, not yet). Before a word like "bedre" (better), it means "even": "Det bliver endnu bedre" (It gets even better).

endskønt.explanation: "Endskønt" means "although": "Endskønt det regnede, gik vi en tur" (Although it rained, we went for a walk). It sounds formal. In everyday talk, use "selvom" (even though): "Selvom det regnede, gik vi en tur" (Even though it rained, we went for a walk).

endvidere.explanation: "Endvidere" means "furthermore". To add one more point to what you just said, say: "Bilen er sikker. Endvidere er den billig" (The car is safe. Furthermore, it is cheap). It sounds formal.

energi.explanation: "Energi" means "energy". To say you feel full of strength, use it too: "Jeg har ikke meget energi i dag" (I do not have much energy today). To talk about electricity from the wall, use "strøm" (electricity): "Der er ingen strøm" (There is no electricity).

energisk.explanation: "Energisk" means "energetic". It comes from "energi" (energy). To say someone has little energy, use the opposite "sløv" (sluggish): "Jeg er sløv i dag" (I am sluggish today).

eneste.explanation: "Eneste" means "only". To say "only" with a number or an amount, use "kun" (just, only) instead: "Jeg har kun én bil" (I have only one car). To say "not a single", put "ikke en" before it: "Der er ikke en eneste sky" (There is not a single cloud).

enestående.explanation: "Enestående" means "unique". It is built from "ene" (alone) and "stående" (standing). To praise someone, say: "Hun har en enestående stemme" (She has an outstanding voice).

engang.explanation: "Engang" means "once". To start a story, say: "Der var engang..." (Once upon a time...). To invite someone for a time you do not name, say: "Kom og besøg mig engang" (Come and visit me sometime). Written as two words, "en gang" means "one time": "en gang om dagen" (once a day).

engelsk.explanation: "Engelsk" means "English". To say you have an English lesson at school, say: "Jeg har engelsk" (I have English). Danish writes words for languages with a lowercase letter: "engelsk", not "Engelsk".

england.explanation: "England" means "England". The country has a capital letter, but "engelsk" (English) does not. To talk about England, Scotland and Wales together, use "Storbritannien" (Great Britain): "Jeg rejser til Storbritannien" (I am travelling to Great Britain).

enhver.explanation: "Enhver" means "every". To say "every day", use "hver" (every) instead: "hver dag" (every day). In front of "barn" (child), it becomes "ethvert": "Ethvert barn kan lære det" (Every child can learn it).

enig.explanation: "Enig" means "agree". Danish uses "er" (am) with it, not a verb: "Jeg er enig" is literally "I am in agreement". To say what you agree with, add "i" (in): "Det er jeg enig i" (I agree with that).

enig med.explanation: "Enig med" means "agree with". To say you agree with a person, use "med" (with): "Jeg er enig med min mor" (I agree with my mom). To say you agree with an idea or opinion, use "enig i" instead: "Jeg er enig i det" (I agree with that).

enkel.explanation: "Enkel" means "simple", as in plain and not complicated. To say something is easy to do, use "let" (easy): "Opgaven er let" (The task is easy).

enkelt.explanation: "Enkelt" means "single". When you say something is not complicated, it means "simple": "Det er enkelt" (It is simple).

enkeltvis.explanation: "Enkeltvis" means "one by one". It is built from "enkelt" (single) and "-vis" (in the way of). The same ending is in "parvis" (in pairs): "De gik parvis ind" (They went in in pairs).

enlig.explanation: "Enlig" means "single", as in living without a partner. To talk about a mother raising children alone, say: "en enlig mor" (a single mother). Do not mix it up with "ensom" (lonely): "Hun føler sig ensom" (She feels lonely).

enogtyve.explanation: "Enogtyve" means "twenty-one". It is built from "en" (one), "og" (and) and "tyve" (twenty), so it is literally "one-and-twenty". Larger numbers follow the same pattern: "toogtyve" (22) and "enogtredive" (31).

enorm.explanation: "Enorm" means "enormous". To say something is only big, use "stor" (big): "Huset er stort" (The house is big).

enormt.explanation: "Enormt" means "enormously". It comes from "enorm" (enormous). To make a describing word much stronger, put it before that word: "Det er enormt dyrt" (It is enormously expensive).

ens.explanation: "Ens" means "identical". To say two people have the same teacher, use "samme" (same) before the noun: "Vi har samme lærer" (We have the same teacher).

ensfarvet.explanation: "Ensfarvet" means "solid-colored". It is built from "ens" (identical) and "farvet" (colored). The opposite is "stribet" (striped): "en stribet trøje" (a striped sweater).

ensomhed.explanation: "Ensomhed" means "loneliness". It is built from "ensom" (lonely) and the ending "-hed" (-ness). To say a person feels lonely, use "ensom": "Jeg føler mig ensom" (I feel lonely).

ental.explanation: "Et ental" means "a singular". It is built from "en" (one) and "tal" (number). The opposite is "et flertal" (a plural): "Ordet bøger er i flertal" (The word bøger is in the plural).

enten.explanation: "Enten" means "either". It works with "eller" (or) to give two choices. To say you take one of two things, say: "Vi tager enten bussen eller toget" (We take either the bus or the train).

enten…eller.explanation: "Enten … eller" means "either … or". To say neither of two things, use "hverken … eller" (neither … nor) instead: "Jeg vil hverken have kaffe eller te" (I want neither coffee nor tea).

entusiastisk.explanation: "Entusiastisk" means "enthusiastic". It comes from "en entusiast" (an enthusiast). To describe a warm welcome, say: "en entusiastisk modtagelse" (an enthusiastic reception).

er det ...?.explanation: "Er det ...?" means "is it ...?". To ask a question, put "er" (is) first, with no extra word like "do": "Er det rigtigt?" (Is that right?).

er du sikker?.explanation: "Er du sikker?" means "are you sure?". To talk about something that cannot hurt you, "sikker" also means "safe": "en sikker bil" (a safe car). To ask more than one person, say: "Er I sikre?" (Are you all sure?).

erfaren.explanation: "Erfaren" means "experienced". It comes from "en erfaring" (experience gained from doing a job). To say in what job, add "som" (as): "Hun er erfaren som kok" (She is experienced as a cook).

et efternavn.explanation: "Et efternavn" means "a last name". It is made of "efter" (after) and "et navn" (a name). To ask for someone's last name, say: "Hvad er dit efternavn?" (What is your last name?).

et efterår.explanation: "Et efterår" means "an autumn". It is made of "efter" (after) and "et år" (a year).

et egern.explanation: "Et egern" means "a squirrel". The plural has the same form as the singular: "to egern" (two squirrels).

et ego.explanation: "Et ego" means "an ego". To say someone thinks too much of himself, say: "Han har et stort ego" (He has a big ego).

et ekko.explanation: "Et ekko" means "an echo". Danish spells it with two k's, "ekko", not "echo".

et eksamensbevis.explanation: "Et eksamensbevis" means "a diploma". It is built from "eksamen" (exam) and "et bevis" (proof).

et eksempel.explanation: "Et eksempel" means "an example". To say "for example", use "for eksempel" (short: "f.eks."): "Jeg kan lide frugt, for eksempel æbler" (I like fruit, for example apples).

et eksperiment.explanation: "Et eksperiment" means "an experiment". It goes with the verb "at eksperimentere" (to experiment). To say someone carries out one, use "udføre" (carry out): "Læreren udfører et eksperiment" (The teacher carries out an experiment).

et emne.explanation: "Et emne" means "a subject / topic". To talk about a school subject like math, use "et fag" (a school subject) instead: "Matematik er mit yndlingsfag" (Math is my favorite subject).

et enkeltværelse.explanation: "Et enkeltværelse" means "a single room". It is made of "enkelt" (single) and "et værelse" (a room). For two people, use "et dobbeltværelse" (a double room): "Vi vil gerne have et dobbeltværelse" (We would like a double room).

et erhverv.explanation: "Et erhverv" means "a profession". To ask what someone does for a living, say: "Hvad er dit erhverv?" (What is your profession?). The word is also part of "erhvervslivet" (the business world): "Hun arbejder i erhvervslivet" (She works in the business world).

et escape room.explanation: "Et escape room" means "an escape room". Danish uses the English words, so it is written the same. To say you have tried one, say: "Vi har været i et escape room" (We have been in an escape room).

et essay.explanation: "Et essay" means "an essay". To talk about a writing task at school, use "en stil" (a composition) instead: "Vi skal skrive en stil" (We have to write a composition).

et eventyr.explanation: "Et eventyr" means "a fairy tale / adventure". To talk about an old story with witches and princes, use it for "a fairy tale": "Hun læser et eventyr for børnene" (She reads a fairy tale to the children). To say a trip was exciting, use it for "an adventure": "Rejsen var et eventyr" (The trip was an adventure).

ethvert.explanation: "Ethvert" means "every". Use it before words like "barn" (child) or "sted" (place). Before words like "mand" (man), use "enhver" (every) instead: "enhver mand" (every man).

etik.explanation: "Etik" means "ethics". To say something is ethical, use "etisk" (ethical): "Det er ikke etisk" (That is not ethical).

eu.explanation: "EU" means "the EU". Danish uses no word for "the" with it: "Danmark er medlem af EU" (Denmark is a member of the EU). Denmark joined in 1973.

europa.explanation: "Europa" means "Europe". The Danish name ends in "a", not "e". To say something belongs to Europe, use "europæisk" (European): "europæisk mad" (European food).

europæisk.explanation: "Europæisk" means "European". It comes from "Europa" (Europe). Unlike English, it is written with a lowercase letter: "europæisk mad" (European food).

eventuel.explanation: "Eventuel" means "possible". To say "any" problems that may or may not come, use it: "Ring, hvis der er eventuelle problemer" (Call if there are any problems). Do not mix it up with English "eventual" (happening in the end). For that, use "til sidst" (in the end): "Til sidst vandt vi" (In the end we won).

evig.explanation: "Evig" means "eternal". To say something seems never to end, use it too: "en evig diskussion" (a never-ending discussion). The noun is "en evighed" (an eternity).

evigt.explanation: "Evigt" means "forever". To say "forever" before a noun, use "evig" (eternal) instead: "evig kærlighed" (eternal love).

at falde.explanation: "At falde" means "to fall". To say rain or snow comes down, use it: "Sneen falder" (The snow is falling). To say someone fell, use the past form "faldt": "Han faldt på isen" (He fell on the ice).

at falde for.explanation: "At falde for" means "to fall for". To say you suddenly love someone or something, use it: "Jeg faldt for hende" (I fell for her). Do not mix it up with plain "at falde" (to fall down): "Sneen falder" (The snow is falling).

at falde i god jord.explanation: "At falde i god jord" means "to go down well". Literally, it means "to fall in good soil", like a seed that will grow. To say a joke was well received, say: "Vittigheden faldt i god jord" (The joke went down well).

at falde i søvn.explanation: "At falde i søvn" means "to fall asleep". Literally, it means "to fall in sleep". To say someone is already asleep, use "at sove" (to sleep): "Hun sover" (She is sleeping).

at falde med næsen i smøret.explanation: "At falde med næsen i smøret" means "to land in clover". Literally, it means "to fall with the nose in the butter".

at falde ned.explanation: "At falde ned" means "to fall down". To say where someone fell down from, add "fra" (from): "Barnet faldt ned fra træet" (The child fell down from the tree).

at falde over.explanation: "At falde over" means "to trip over / come across". To say you trip on something while walking, use it: "Jeg faldt over en sten" (I tripped over a stone). To say you find something by chance, use it too: "Jeg faldt over en gammel bog" (I came across an old book).

at falde til ro.explanation: "At falde til ro" means "to calm down". To say a child calms down, say: "Barnet faldt til ro" (The child calmed down). To calm someone else, use "at berolige" (to soothe): "Jeg beroliger barnet" (I soothe the child).

at fange.explanation: "At fange" means "to catch". To say you catch something moving, use it: "Politiet fanger tyven" (The police catch the thief). To say you catch a bus or train, use "at nå" (to make it) instead: "Jeg når toget" (I catch the train).

at fare.explanation: "At fare" means "to rush". To say something shot past, use the past form "for": "Bilen for forbi" (The car shot past). Do not mix it up with the small word "for" (for): "Gaven er for dig" (The gift is for you).

at fare vild.explanation: "At fare vild" means "to get lost". To say you lost a thing, use "at miste" (to lose) instead: "Jeg mistede min nøgle" (I lost my key). "Vild" means "wild" in other words: "vilde dyr" (wild animals).

at farve.explanation: "At farve" means "to color / dye". To say you change your hair color, say: "Hun farver sit hår" (She is dyeing her hair). To say you color in a picture, use it too: "Børnene farver tegningen" (The children are coloring the drawing).

at faste.explanation: "At faste" means "to fast". To talk about Lent, the time before Easter, use "fasten" (Lent): "Fasten begynder før påske" (Lent begins before Easter).

at fastholde.explanation: "At fastholde" means "to maintain / hold on to". It is built from "fast" (firm) and "at holde" (to hold). To say you do not change your opinion, say: "at fastholde sin mening" (to stick to your opinion).

at fastslå.explanation: "At fastslå" means "to establish / determine". To say someone states a fact after checking, say: "Politiet har fastslået, at han var alene" (The police have established that he was alone).

at fastsætte.explanation: "At fastsætte" means "to fix / set". To say you choose a date, say: "at fastsætte en dato" (to set a date). To state a fact that is already true, use "at fastslå" (to establish) instead: "Eksperterne fastslår årsagen" (The experts establish the cause).

at fatte.explanation: "At fatte" means "to grasp / understand". To ask if someone understands, say: "Fatter du det?" (Do you get it?). To say you make a decision, use it with "en beslutning" (a decision): "Vi fatter en beslutning" (We make a decision).

at feje.explanation: "At feje" means "to sweep". To clean a wet floor, use "at vaske" (to wash) instead: "Jeg vasker gulvet" (I wash the floor).

at feje noget ind under gulvtæppet.explanation: "At feje noget ind under gulvtæppet" means "to sweep the problem under the rug". Literally, it means "to sweep something in under the floor carpet". To say a company hides a mistake, say: "Firmaet fejer fejlen ind under gulvtæppet" (The company sweeps the mistake under the rug).
